creator: Alexander Terp
description:
Rad can already be sandboxed for everything except the filesystem, and that gap is one an embedder cannot work around.

RunnerInput (core/global.go) is a complete dependency-injection struct: stdio, exit, HTTP, shell, clock, sleep, signals, confirm, terminal, home, terminal width. Every outside-world edge is a seam, so a host can already deny shell and network per invocation. That is most of a capability model, already built.

The filesystem escaped the rule. Probed with real scripts through an embedded runtime:

| Call | Result | Blockable today |
|---|---|---|
| shell out via dollar-backtick | executed, file created | **yes** - an injected deny-all RShell intercepted it, exit 126, never ran |
| read_file("/etc/hosts") | read 300 bytes | no |
| write_file("/tmp/rad_pwned.txt") | file created with content | no |
| get_env("HOME") | "/Users/amterp" | no |

The call sites go straight to os.* with no seam: core/funcs.go:1136 (ReadFile), :1182 and :1191 (OpenFile, WriteFile), :815 (Getenv), core/func_mkdir.go:30, and :920 **os.RemoveAll**, which means a hostile script can recursively delete. HTTP is adjacent: RReq is a concrete *Requester (core/requester.go:23) rather than an interface, so it cannot be substituted either.

## Why this matters beyond nook

"Can I safely run a Rad script someone sent me" is a question every scripting language eventually has to answer, and today the answer is no.

AGENTS.md already mandates that I/O go through the core/global.go seams. The filesystem simply escaped it, so this closes a gap in an existing design rather than introducing a new concept.

For nook it decides whether third-party Rad plugins can exist at all. Until it lands, Rad plugins are trusted-only, which puts the tier meant to showcase Rad behind the tier that needs no trust.

## Shape

Add an RFs interface seam, route the ~10 os.* sites through it, make RReq an interface, and add capability flags to RunnerInput so a host can express what a script may touch. Contained and idiomatic - it follows the pattern the other twelve seams already use.

One note for whoever picks this up: for untrusted scripts, in-process embedding is worse than a subprocess, not better. No OS boundary, and nothing to wrap in sandbox-exec.
title: Give the filesystem an injectable seam, and add capability flags
